title: How to screen new sign-ups without adding friction
summary: How to screen new sign-ups without adding friction: research the name, email and phone users already give. Sixtyfour does it in the background, with sources.
body_markdown:
Keep the sign-up form as it is and research the details users already give, such as their name, email address, phone number, employer and profile link, in the background once they have signed up. Clear the accounts whose details lead to one real person, send the ones whose details contradict each other or stay open to a person on your team, and ask only those few for anything more. Run the same research again before payouts and other risky steps.


It means screening new users with information you already have, so most genuine users never meet an extra step such as an ID upload, a selfie or a code. Each of those steps is a point where someone with nothing to hide can stop, often without telling you why. Background research screens everyone, and the extra steps go only to the accounts that need them.


Check whether the details belong to one real person who existed before today: the email address can receive mail and leads to the person named, the phone number leads to the same person, and the employer and profile they gave exist and agree. A contradiction, such as an address that leads to someone else, is the strongest flag. Signals collected from the device and network, which other tools handle, catch automated and repeat sign-ups.


No. Young people, recent arrivals and people who keep off the internet on purpose often have little online, so a thin footprint is a reason to look more closely or to ask. On its own it should not decide an account. Contradictions between the details a person gave are a far stronger signal than absence.


Ask when the background research leaves a question open that a document answers, such as whether the person is who they say they are, and the account is about to do something costly to get wrong, such as receive a payout or meet people in person. Ask for that one thing, say why, and let the person keep using the parts of your product that carry no risk while they answer.


Yes. Sixtyfour is a research API that takes the name, email address, phone number or profile link a new user gave, researches sources across the web in the background, and returns the answers you ask for, such as whether the details belong to one person, with each finding's source and, when you ask for one, a 0 to 100 confidence score. Your rules decide which accounts a person reviews, and anything the research could not establish is reported as open for your team to decide.
